---
title: Why are the Guianas divided five ways?
summary: How the coast between the Orinoco and the Amazon ended up with five owners — footholds between two empires, owners fixed by the date of a peace, Humboldt on the river two degrees away, which branch is the river, and the Essequibo case at the ICJ.
date: 2026-11-13
tags: [history]
distillate: The Guianas were not one colony split five ways but five footholds at river mouths, taken by latecomers on the coast that Spain and Portugal, holding the Orinoco and the Amazon, had left empty. European peace treaties fixed each owner by what it held on a date, and drew the interior by naming rivers that nobody had surveyed or settled. Every land boundary in the region was then disputed, and in four of the five disputes the question was which river a text meant; the fifth, Venezuela's claim to the land west of the Essequibo, about two-thirds of Guyana, turns on whether old title or possession counts, and was argued on the merits at the International Court of Justice in May 2026.
model: [Claude Opus 5.5]
---

The Guianas are the stretch of South American coast between the mouth of the Orinoco and the
mouth of the Amazon. From west to east the region now belongs to Venezuela (its Guayana region
and the Orinoco delta), Guyana (once British Guiana), Suriname (once Dutch Guiana), French
Guiana, still part of France, and Brazil's state of Amapá, once called Portuguese Guiana
("The Guianas"). Five owners for one stretch of coast needs explaining. This note takes a
position on why: the region fragmented because it
was taken from the sea, river mouth by river mouth, by powers that never held its interior, and
every boundary between them was later drawn by a text naming a river or a date rather than by
anyone on the ground.

The evidence is the treaties and awards themselves, and one letter of advice: Alexander von
Humboldt's memoir of 1817 on the boundary between French and Portuguese Guiana, written for the
negotiators who had to apply the peace of Vienna. Quotations are given in the original with a
translation; translations are our own.

## Five boundaries, five texts

Throughout, the note returns to one table: each land boundary of the region, the text that first
fixed it, and what the parties later disputed. The map after it marks the five disputes.

| Boundary | Fixed by | The text names | Disputed | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Venezuela–Guyana | award under the Treaty of Washington, 1899 | the Dutch and Spanish holdings when Britain took the colony | Essequibo river or the Schomburgk line | award of 1899; rejected by Venezuela since 1962; at the ICJ |
| Guyana–Suriname | Anglo-Dutch convention, 1814 | the Corentyne | which branch is the Corentyne: Kutari or New River | unsettled; Guyana holds the triangle |
| Suriname–French Guiana | Dutch and French officials, 1836 | the Maroni | which branch is the Lawa: Litani or Marouini | Tsar's award, 1891, for the Lawa; the headwaters still open |
| French Guiana–Brazil | Treaty of Utrecht, 1713 | the "Japoc or Vincent Pinçon" | which river is the Japoc: Oyapock or Araguari | Swiss award, 1900, for Brazil |
| Guyana–Brazil | no treaty before 1901 | (the Schomburgk survey) | the Pirara district | King of Italy's award, 1904, split it |

Two things stand out. Every one of these boundaries was disputed after it was fixed, and four
of the five disputes are the same question asked of different rivers: which stream did the
text mean? The sixth land boundary, between Brazil and Suriname, was fixed by a treaty signed
in Rio de Janeiro on 5 May 1906 (Costa Franco), and no dispute over it appears in the sources
used here.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 285" role="img" aria-label="Map of the Guianas from the Orinoco delta to the Amazon mouth, showing Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and Brazil's Amapá state. Three shaded areas are still claimed today: the Essequibo region west of the Essequibo river, claimed by Venezuela; the New River Triangle in southern Guyana and the Marouini tract in southern French Guiana, both claimed by Suriname. Numbered markers also show the Pirara district on the Guyana–Brazil border, split in 1904, and the land between the Oyapock and Araguari rivers in Amapá, which France lost in 1900." xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto;">

*The Guianas today, with the five boundary disputes. Shaded areas are still claimed by a
neighbour. Boundaries, rivers and disputed areas are from Natural Earth (1:10 million); the
markers for Pirara and the Oyapock–Araguari land are placed by hand and are approximate.*

## Footholds between two empires

The region had no single owner to divide, because the two powers with the strongest paper
claim never settled it. Spain held the Orinoco and Portugal the Amazon, the two rivers that
carried traffic inland, and the old name for the whole region, the "Island of Guiana", was the
land enclosed by the Orinoco, the Rio Negro and the Amazon ("The Guianas"). The coast between
the two river mouths was left to latecomers, who came by sea and stayed at the mouths of
smaller rivers: the Dutch on the Essequibo, where Aert Adriaenszoon Groenewegen built Fort
Kyk-Over-Al in 1616, and on the Berbice in 1627; the English on the Suriname in 1651; the
French at Cayenne, whose settlement was unstable until 1643 ("The Guianas"; "Guayana
Esequiba"). Each began as a separate plantation colony with its own river, and none was ever
the province of a larger one.

Humboldt, who had travelled the Orinoco and the Rio Negro, describes what lay behind these
coasts in 1817:

> J’ai vu de près ces pays déserts dont les souverains de l’Europe se disputent la possession sur la carte. […] Cette culture ne marche que lentement des côtes vers l’intérieur […]
>
> "I have seen close up these empty lands whose possession the sovereigns of Europe dispute on the map. […] Cultivation advances only slowly from the coasts toward the interior."

Humboldt's
French keeps the spelling of his day: he writes *étoit*, *françoise* and *hollandois* where
French now writes *était*, *française* and *hollandais*. "Empty" is a European's word: the
interior had Indigenous peoples, and between the Maroni and the Essequibo Humboldt himself
places the "nègres révoltés du Surinam", the Maroons who had escaped slavery. What it lacked
was any European presence, so a European claim to it could rest only on a text.

## Owners fixed by the date of a peace

The number of owners was settled not by anyone's plan for the region but by the European wars
in which its colonies changed hands, and by peace treaties that confirmed whoever held what on a
given day.

The first was the peace of Breda, signed on 31 July 1667 between England and the Dutch
Republic. Its Article 3 applied *uti possidetis*, "as you possess", with an effective date of
20 May 1667: each side kept what it held then. The Dutch held Suriname, which Abraham Crijnssen
had taken from the English earlier that year, and the English held New Netherland ("Treaty of Breda (1667)"; "The Guianas"). Breda is often
told as a swap of Suriname for New York. The rule, as Wikipedia summarizes Article 3, says
something narrower: neither side handed anything over, and Suriname stayed Dutch because the
Dutch held it on the cut-off date.

The second set came at the end of the French wars. Britain took control of the Dutch colonies
in 1796, after France invaded the Dutch Republic ("Guyana"). By the convention of London of
13 August 1814, the Dutch ceded Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice to Britain, and Britain
returned Suriname ("Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814"). The three colonies Britain kept became one
colony, British Guiana, in 1831 ("Guyana"). Meanwhile Portugal, from Brazil, had occupied French
Guiana in January 1809, and the Congress of Vienna made it return the colony, which a French
fleet took back on 8 November 1817 ("Invasion of Cayenne (1809)").

Each of these peaces froze a pattern of occupation on the coast rather than redrawing it. On
this reading the count of five records where European wars left things, not any feature of the
land: the Dutch colonies west of Suriname became British because Britain held them when the
war ended, and the boundary between the British and Dutch colonies was put on the Corentyne
("Tigri Area"). The coast was divided by possession. The interior, which nobody possessed, was divided by
words, and that is where the disputes came.

## A river two degrees away

The boundary between French Guiana and Brazil shows how a word could carry a dispute for two
centuries. The treaty of Utrecht between France and Portugal, signed on 11 April 1713, set the
limit at the river "Japoc ou Vincent Pinçon", and France gave up the lands between it and the
Amazon.[^utrecht] The trouble is that the two names may describe two different rivers. In 1817,
asked for advice on article 107 of the Vienna act, Humboldt put it this way:

> L’art. 8 du traité d’Utrecht étoit très-vaguement énoncé. La cession va jusqu’au Rio Japoc ou Vincent Pinçon; or, il y a une différence de près de deux degrés en latitude entre le Rio Pinçon et le Rio Japoc ou Oyapock, appelé anciennement Wiapoco par les navigateurs hollandois.

"Article 8 of the treaty of Utrecht was very vaguely worded. The cession runs to the Rio Japoc
or Vincent Pinçon; but there is a difference of nearly two degrees of latitude between the Rio
Pinçon and the Rio Japoc or Oyapock, formerly called Wiapoco by the Dutch navigators." Two
degrees of latitude is about 220 km, north to south. Humboldt then offers a reason for the error:

> L’erreur commise par les négociateurs de la paix d’Utrecht peut avoir été fondée sur les fausses dénominations des caps de cette côte. L’Oyapock débouche au nord du cap Orange, comme le Rio Pinçon au nord du cap Nord; or, jusqu’à la fin du 17e siècle, les géographes donnoient quelquefois le nom de cap Nord au cap Orange.

"The error made by the negotiators of the peace of Utrecht may have come from the wrong names
of the capes on this coast. The Oyapock flows out north of Cape Orange, as the Rio Pinçon does
north of Cape North; but until the end of the 17th century, geographers sometimes gave the name
Cape North to Cape Orange." He backs this with Laet's *Americae utriusque descriptio* (1633), which
he quotes in Latin: the cape closing the bay of the Wiapoco "is called by the English *cabo de
Corde*, by our people *cap d'Orange*, and not rarely *cabo di Nord*". If two capes shared a name, two rivers could share one too.

Read closely, the passage does two things. It concedes that the treaty is ambiguous, which was
the French case, and it explains the ambiguity as a mapmakers' confusion, which favoured the
Portuguese reading that the negotiators meant the Oyapock. Humboldt then argues that the
question had been closed anyway, by the words of the Vienna act, which he quotes (the print repeats « at the start of each line, dropped here):

> «On restituera jusqu’à la rivière d’Oyapock dont l’embouchure est située entre les 4e et 5e degrés de latitude septentrionale, limite que le Portugal a toujours considérée comme celle qui avoit été fixée par le traité d’Utrecht.» Ces mots, limite qui.... ont été ajoutés pour qu’il ne soit plus question du Rio Vincent Pinçon […]

"'The territory will be restored up to the river Oyapock, whose mouth lies between the 4th and
5th degrees of northern latitude, a limit that Portugal has always considered to be the one
fixed by the treaty of Utrecht.' These words, *a limit that…*, were added so that there would
no longer be any question of the Rio Vincent Pinçon." Humboldt read the clause as the
Portuguese did. But the clause says only what Portugal had always *considered*; France had not
agreed to that reading, and it reopened the question.

France pressed its claim through the 19th century. Its troops occupied part of today's Amapá in
1835, and the two states neutralized the territory in 1841 (Costa Franco). After more incidents,
including an armed clash there in 1895 ("Amapá Question"), a treaty signed in Rio de Janeiro on
10 April 1897 sent the question to the Swiss Federal Council (Costa Franco). Brazil's case was argued by
the Baron of Rio Branco in two memoirs, of five and six volumes, with maps and documents (Costa
Franco). The question put to the arbitrator was Humboldt's question: France held that the Japoc
of Utrecht was the Araguari, which reaches the sea south of Cape North, and claimed the interior
west to the Rio Branco; Brazil held that it was the Oyapock ("Questão do Amapá"). On 1 December
1900 Walter Hauser, president of the Swiss Confederation, decided for Brazil:

> conforme o sentido preciso do artigo 8 do Tratado de Utrecht, o rio Yapoc ou Vicente Pinsão é o Oiapoque, que se lança no oceano imediatamente a oeste do Cabo Orange

"according to the precise meaning of article 8 of the treaty of Utrecht, the river Yapoc or
Vicente Pinsão is the Oyapock, which flows into the ocean immediately west of Cape Orange."
This is the award as quoted in Portuguese by Costa Franco, who spells the arbitrator's name
"Heuser"; the French original was not opened for this note. For the interior the award took the
watershed of the Amazon basin, along the Tumuc-Humac mountains ("Questão do Amapá"), the kind of
limit Humboldt had recommended in 1817. In Guiana, he wrote, the courses of rivers, mountain
chains and watersheds made the best boundaries: "le cours des rivières, les chaînes des
montagnes, les partages d’eau m’auroient paru présenter les limites les plus avantageuses".

How much land the word "Japoc" carried depends on which French claim is counted. The historian
Stéphane Granger, quoted by *Slate*, gives about 80,000 km² between the Oyapock and the
Araguari; Portuguese Wikipedia gives 550,000 km² for the whole contested territory, which adds
the French claim west to the Rio Branco ("Questão do Amapá"). The
two figures are not in conflict: the first is the coastal strip, the second the coast plus the
paper interior.

## Which branch is the river

The two boundaries of Suriname show the same problem one step further inland. Here everyone
agreed on the river; the question was which of its branches the river was.

**The Corentyne.** The 1814 settlement put the boundary between British and Dutch Guiana on the
Corentyne. Its upper course splits, and the parties disagree on whether the Kutari or the New
River is the Corentyne's source. Robert Schomburgk, surveying for Britain, went up the Kutari
in 1840 and took it to be the source; Charles Barrington Brown found the larger New River, or
Upper Corentyne, in 1871 ("Tigri Area"). Between the two branches lies the New River Triangle,
about 14,400 km² on the map's data, or 7% of Guyana. A mixed commission in 1936 gave the
triangle to British Guiana, but the treaty was never ratified because the Second World War
broke out. After both countries became independent the dispute became armed: on 19 August 1969
Guyanese forces took Camp Tigri from Surinamese militias, and Guyana holds the area today
("Tigri Area").

**The Maroni.** Dutch and French officials set the boundary on the Maroni in 1836. Upstream the
Maroni is the Lawa, and above that the Lawa forks again. Tsar Alexander III, as arbitrator,
ruled in May 1891 that the Lawa was the boundary, which settled the larger fork in the Dutch
favour. Which of the Lawa's own branches, the Litani (Itany) or the Marouini, continues the
line was left open, and the tract between them is still claimed by Suriname; in 2021 the two
governments agreed on about two-thirds of the river boundary ("France–Suriname border").[^marouini]

**Pirara.** The Guyana–Brazil boundary had no old text at all, and it shows what happened when
neither side could point to one. Britain claimed the Pirara district on the strength of
Schomburgk's surveys of 1835–1840 and of an alleged old Dutch post on the upper Essequibo;
Brazil had a fort on the Rio Branco and a post on the Pirara itself. The two neutralized the district by an exchange
of notes in 1842 and, by a treaty of 6 November 1901, sent it to the King of Italy, Victor
Emmanuel III (Costa Franco). His award, dated 6 June 1904, split the territory instead of
choosing between the claims. Portuguese Wikipedia gives the result as 19,630 km² to Britain and
13,570 km² to Brazil ("Questão do Pirara"), so Britain received 59% of the 33,200 km² divided.
Costa Franco writes that the king ignored the parties' arguments and gave Brazil less than
Britain had offered in direct talks. In the one dispute with no old text to interpret, the
arbitrator split the difference.

## Essequibo: possession written into the rules

The largest dispute is the only one that is not about a river's identity. Venezuela claims all
the land west of the Essequibo river, about two-thirds of Guyana. Its argument is from Spanish
title: when Spain created the Captaincy General of Venezuela in 1777, the Essequibo was restated
as the natural border ("Guayana Esequiba"). Britain's argument was from Dutch and then British
possession, which reached west of the Essequibo. Robert Schomburgk drew a boundary in 1840; a
version extended westward appeared only in 1886, when Britain declared it the provisional
frontier, and Venezuela broke off relations in 1887. Gold found in the Cuyuni basin from 1876
raised the stakes, and the United States pressed Britain to arbitrate in 1895 ("Schomburgk
Line"; "Venezuela Crisis of 1895").

The Treaty of Washington, signed on 2 February 1897, set the rules. Article III told the
tribunal to "investigate and ascertain the extent of the territories" held by the Netherlands
and by Spain when Britain acquired its colony, and then to draw the line. Article IV gave the
first rule for doing so:

> Adverse holding or prescription during a period of fifty years shall make a good title.

This sentence is the heart of the case. Elsewhere in the Guianas the arbitrators asked what a
text meant. Here the treaty told them that occupation for fifty years was title in itself,
whatever a Spanish decree of 1777 said. Of the two kinds of claim in play, Spain's paper title
and the possession built up by the Dutch and British, the rule could only help the side that
had possessed. The tribunal (two British judges, two American judges chosen for Venezuela, and
the Russian jurist Friedrich Martens as umpire) gave a unanimous award on 3 October 1899 without
stating reasons. It largely restored the Schomburgk line, with two changes for Venezuela: Barima
Point at the mouth of the Orinoco, and the boundary on the Wenamu instead of the Cuyuni. Britain
kept almost 90% of the disputed territory and all of the gold mines ("Paris Arbitral Award";
RIAA, vol. XXVIII). A boundary agreement with Venezuela followed in 1905 (Guyana, 2 May 2026).

Venezuela's rejection rests on events after the award. Severo Mallet-Prevost, a lawyer for
Venezuela at the tribunal, left a memorandum written in 1944 for publication after his death;
it appeared in 1949. It alleges that Martens offered the American judges a choice between a
unanimous award and a three-to-two award more favourable to Britain, as part of a political deal
between Russia and Britain. The allegation is one man's account written forty-five years later,
and Wikipedia notes that the papers of the five arbitrators do not substantiate it ("Mallet-Prevost
memorandum"). Venezuela declared before the United Nations in 1962 that it no longer
accepted the award ("Guayana Esequiba").

The Geneva Agreement of 17 February 1966, signed by Britain, British Guiana and Venezuela, is
worth reading for what it does not say. Its first article sets up a
mixed commission to settle the controversy "which has arisen as the result of the Venezuelan
contention that the Arbitral Award of 1899 about the frontier between British Guiana and
Venezuela is null and void." The agreement records a *contention*. It does not say the award is
void, and it does not say it is valid; Article V adds that nothing in it is a "renunciation or
diminution" of either side's claim (UNTS 561). Each side has since read it its own way. Guyana
relies on the award and the 1905 boundary agreement (Guyana, 2 May 2026); Venezuela argued at
the court in 2026 that the Geneva Agreement had replaced the award (Guyana, 7 May 2026).

Two figures for the size of the claim are in use: 159,500 km² (Wikipedia, "Guayana Esequiba"),
which is 74% of Guyana's 214,969 km², and about 143,000 km² measured on the map's data, which
is 67% of Guyana's 212,139 km² there. Either way it is between two-thirds and three-quarters of
the country.

## Where the Essequibo case stands

As of November 2026. Guyana filed its application at the International Court of Justice on
29 March 2018, asking the court to confirm the 1899 award. The court held that it had
jurisdiction on 18 December 2020 and rejected Venezuela's preliminary objection on 6 April 2023
(ICJ, case 171). After Venezuela announced a referendum on the territory, the court ordered on
1 December 2023 that Venezuela refrain from any action that would modify the situation, in which
Guyana administers the area; the referendum went ahead two days later, with official results
of over 95% "yes" and a turnout that observers doubted, and in March 2024 Venezuela passed a law
making the territory a Venezuelan state ("Guyana–Venezuela crisis"). The court issued a second
order on provisional measures on 1 May 2025 (ICJ, case 171).

The hearings on the merits ran from 4 to 11 May 2026. Venezuela took part, while saying that
its participation did not recognize the court's jurisdiction, and argued that the award was the
product of fraud and collusion; Guyana asked the court to affirm the award's validity and
binding effect (Guyana, 2 and 7 May 2026; "Guyana–Venezuela relations"). Guyana's foreign
ministry expected the judgment at the end of 2026; none had been given when this note was
written.

## Where the sources are thin

The primary texts behind this note are of three kinds, and each has its slant. The treaties
were written by the parties to them, in Europe, about places their signatories had not seen.
The awards were written by arbitrators who, in 1899 and 1904, gave few or no reasons, so their
logic has to be inferred from the line they drew. Humboldt's memoir is advice to an unnamed
correspondent who had sent him a map drawn in the military archives at Rio de Janeiro in 1816;
he calls himself "entièrement étranger à la connoissance des affaires diplomatiques",
a stranger to diplomacy, and his reading of the Vienna act
matches the Portuguese one, though he also sets out what he would object if he were defending
France.

Much of the rest comes through summaries: Wikipedia for the treaties of Breda and London, the
Tigri and Marouini disputes and the Essequibo history, and the Brazilian diplomatic historian
Costa Franco for the Amapá and Pirara cases. Costa Franco writes from the Brazilian side and
praises Rio Branco's defence; his description of the 1904 award as ignoring the parties'
arguments is Brazil's view of a case Brazil lost. The Mallet-Prevost memorandum, central to
Venezuela's case, is known here only through Wikipedia's account, and the court has not yet
said what weight it gives it. Numbers for areas differ between sources by a tenth or more,
because the disputed areas have no surveyed edges.

The argument would be weakened by a boundary in the region that was settled by occupation of the
interior rather than by a text, or by a dispute about a coast that both sides had settled.
Essequibo comes closest to the second: the land west of the river was settled by the Dutch and
British, and the dispute is over whether that settlement made title. But even there the
question the tribunal answered was set by a text, the fifty-year rule, and Venezuela's
objection is to the tribunal, not to any rival settlement on the ground.

## Summary

The Guianas were divided five ways because they were never one colony. Spain and Portugal held
the Orinoco and the Amazon and left the coast between them to the Dutch, English and French,
who settled at separate river mouths. European peace treaties then fixed the owners by what each
held on a date, at Breda in 1667, London in 1814 and Vienna in 1815, and drew the inland
boundaries by naming rivers. Because no one occupied the interior, each named river became a
dispute: which river was the Japoc, which branch was the Corentyne or the Lawa. Arbitrators
settled the Japoc in 1900 and split Pirara in 1904; the Corentyne and Lawa headwaters are still
open. The one dispute of another kind, Essequibo, was decided in 1899 by a rule that counted
fifty years of possession as title, and it is the one now before the International Court of
Justice.
